rationale: Attached foraminifera are often flattened on the side fixed to the substrate, and Globigerina is trochospiral, but trochospiral coiling is widespread among both benthic and planktonic spiral forms, so a majority of plane spirals is not supported. An unspecified force holding chambers in one plane is not the accepted control on coiling.

Some foraminifera, including Peneroplis, are morphologically plastic, but molecular work finds many morphospecies hide distinct lineages rather than genera being transient surface-energy variants. Slight changes in surface energy are not the mechanism that turns one named form into another.

Foraminiferal test shape is tied to microhabitat, buoyancy, and dissolution resistance, and many lineages vanished at mass extinctions, so forms are not equally fit. Long persistence of some body plans does not imply the absence of selection.

Planktonic foraminifera repeatedly re-evolve similar chamber arrangements and keeled or globular morphotypes in separate lineages through the Cenozoic. Morphospace is constrained enough that close homeomorphs arise independently, even if the copies are not strictly identical.

Delicate tests do accumulate unbroken in deep-sea ooze, so crushing is not a constant hazard for every species. Wall thickness and architecture still vary with predation, abrasion, and carbonate saturation, so strength is sometimes a selective factor.

Empty tests are hydraulically equivalent to fine sediment and are winnowed from high-energy gravels, which is the usual reason dead assemblages are scarce there. Living foraminifera also avoid some coarse bottoms, but current sorting accounts for the main sedimentary pattern.

When form is tightly constrained by mechanics or development, similar shapes evolve repeatedly and are weak evidence of kinship on their own. Modern systematics treats that homoplasy as a reason to revise morphology-only phylogenies.

A rhinoceros horn is a keratin mass added at the base and typically curves backward in the median plane, which a steady excess of anterior over posterior growth would produce as an equiangular spiral. Real horns are abraded and only approximately logarithmic, so the constant-ratio idealization is good but not exact.

Paired bovid horns are bilateral enantiomorphs: the left horn is the mirror image of the right in a normally developed animal. Injury and rare developmental asymmetry create exceptions without upsetting the general rule.

Many bovid horns are well approximated by a twisted logarithmic spiral produced by unequal growth around the base. Seasonal growth, age-related changes in curvature, and some horns closer to a circular helix or a nearly straight cone mean a constant-ratio logarithmic spiral is not the form of the great majority throughout life.

Straight oryx horns correspond to a small spiral angle and tightly coiled ram horns to a larger one, so the ordering of the series is plausible. The stated degree values are specimen-level measurements, not established species constants, and oryx sits outside the goat and sheep comparison.

Argali and Marco Polo sheep horns share a broadly similar open coil and differ conspicuously in how far the horn flares and twists away from the head. Whether the equiangular constant is nearly identical, with the helical component carrying almost all the difference, is a reasonable description that has not been shown as a precise species rule.

If the fastest and slowest growth lie opposite each other, curvature stays in one plane; an offset between them adds torsion and a space spiral. Most hollow horns lack that symmetry and are helical rather than planar.

Unequal drag of the sheath on the bony core is kinematically capable of bending a horn the same way unequal growth does. Horn shape is produced mainly by localized keratin production over the germinal epithelium and by the shape of the core, so adhesion is not established as the chief cause.

A wider growth zone can translate a given growth gradient into a larger length difference, which could tighten a curve. Thick horns are not in general more strongly spiraled than slender ones: oryx horns are stout and nearly straight, while some narrower horns are markedly curved.

Non-circular prisms do warp under torsion in the way Saint-Venant described, and sheep horns show sinuous growth lines that cylindrical cattle horns largely lack. Those lines record the contour of the germinative epithelium through seasonal growth, and torsional strain of an attached sheath is not shown to be their cause.

Circumnutation is produced by a migrating zone of faster elongation, so the stem bends because opposite sides grow at unequal rates, and that growth is distributed along the elongating internode rather than at a single base. The comparison with a horn is kinematic; the oscillation itself is physiologically regulated.

Friction with a rough support can apply a couple to a twining stem and contribute to twisting of the axis. Stem torsion also occurs as part of intrinsic circumnutation, and added rigidity from a twisted axis is a real mechanical effect, so adhesion does not make an adaptive account unnecessary.

A pair of antlers is roughly mirror-symmetric and the tines occupy a curved volume around the head. They are not confined to one smooth spheroidal or ellipsoidal surface, and an antler is a branching beam rather than essentially a surface.

Structures that lengthen by permanent addition with a constant excess of growth on one side of the axis follow an equiangular spiral, and claws, beaks, and ever-growing teeth commonly show that curve once they are long enough. The ratio of growth is not always constant, so the spiral is a strong tendency rather than an invariable outcome.

Elephant, mastodon, and mammoth tusks are all curved dentine, but mammoth tusks are more strongly spiraled and twisted, and living species differ in curvature by species and sex. Extra length on a living elephant tusk would extend its own curve, not reproduce the mammoth spiral.

The same lattice of primordia appears as helices on a cylinder and as logarithmic spirals once that surface is shortened into a cone, ellipsoid, or disk. Fir cones, teasels, thistles, and sunflower heads are standard examples of that geometric series.

Regularly timed, similarly placed primordia do generate helical and spiral lattices as a geometric consequence. The particular divergence near the golden angle is selected by inhibitory fields and packing, so the pattern is not a necessary result of regular intervals alone.

Two logarithmic spirals about one pole meet at a constant angle fixed by their spiral angles, and a right angle is only the special case in which those angles differ by 90 degrees. Visible parastichies in capitula commonly meet obliquely.

Contact parastichies are often stable within a conifer species, and larch cones commonly show five and eight. Norway spruce cones are also typically five and eight, not five and three, and a substantial minority of larch cones depart from the modal pair.

On a capitulum the visible Fibonacci pair rises as more florets are packed into a larger disk. Pairs such as 34/55, 55/89, and 89/144 are the ordinary sequence reported for sunflowers of increasing size.

Spiral phyllotaxis within a species is split about evenly between the two handednesses, with only small biases in some plants. A count of 224 right-handed against 243 left-handed spruce cones is the sort of near-even split that repeated surveys find.

On a single generative spiral, each lattice point belongs to every parastichy family, so a visible Fibonacci pair implies the lower pairs as families of curves through the same points. Those lower families need not be the conspicuous contact spirals.

The golden divergence places about 2.6 leaves on one turn of the genetic spiral, and most alternate spiral systems fall between two and three leaves per turn, which yields Fibonacci parastichies. Plants cluster near that specific angle rather than filling the whole interval, and the less common series do sit near three, four, or five leaves per turn.

Which Fibonacci pair is the contact pair changes with the radial spacing and the shape of the primordium. The divergence angle still decides which number series appears, so conspicuousness is not independent of divergence.

The continued-fraction approach of the Fibonacci ratios to the golden mean is the mathematical reason a divergence near 137.5 degrees packs successive primordia with minimal overlap. That angle is an attractor of primordium-placement dynamics and is biologically significant; orthostichies are the secondary feature.

Distichous, decussate, and low-order spiral shoots are more widespread than sunflower-scale parastichy numbers. Measured divergence in spiral systems clusters near the golden angle even when the visible counts are small, so poor classical fractions do not show that close approximations are rare.

On a long shoot, increasing internode length separates leaves more effectively than a small change in azimuth. In rosettes, cones, and capitula the divergence controls overlap, so it remains a real means of spacing.

Fibonacci phyllotaxis is a standard botanical pattern, produced by local inhibitory interactions and efficient at packing. Both the series and hypotheses about its advantage belong in the explanation of plant form.

Bird, crocodile, and hard-shelled tortoise eggs are spherical to elongate, with length at least as great as breadth, and are approximately surfaces of revolution. Flattened or discoidal hard-shelled eggs are not known in these groups, though many eggs are asymmetric rather than true spheroids.

Egg shape is set while the shell membrane is still flexible, by oviduct pressure together with membrane thickness and stiffness, and calcification then preserves that form. Broad comparisons find little support for nest type as the main cause, while flight-related body shape is associated with the pressure and membrane conditions.

Guillemots, sandpipers, and terns combine large eggs with strong posterior taper, and the kiwi’s very large egg is comparatively elliptical. Across birds, asymmetry tracks flight-related anatomy more closely than relative egg size, so greater oviduct pressure on large eggs is not the general rule.

A pullet’s first eggs are smaller than those she lays after the reproductive tract matures, and very small early eggs are often rounder. Systematic comparisons find little consistent shape difference between the pullet year and later years, and the breed-level link between small eggs and round eggs is only partial.

Asymmetric eggs form where muscular pressure and a nonuniform membrane make one end blunter than the other, and the blunt end is the anterior end in the oviduct. A single peristaltic peak behind the middle is a simplification of that pressure field, and the taper’s role in travel is secondary to the membrane mechanics.

Balance of a fluid-filled membrane requires internal pressure to equal external pressure plus tension times the sum of the principal curvatures, which is Laplace’s relation. Real shell membranes have uneven thickness and tension, and the rigid shell no longer obeys that equilibrium, so it is a first-order description rather than the equation of every egg.

For a given pressure jump, membrane tension is lower where mean curvature is higher, so the sharply curved small end is not the expected site of greatest tension. Irregularities of abnormal eggs are not established to concentrate there.

Schistosoma mansoni, with a lateral egg spine and Biomphalaria hosts, and S. haematobium, with a terminal spine and Bulinus hosts, are separate species by adult anatomy, life cycle, and genetics. Spine position is a species character, not a molding variant of one worm.

Regular echinoid tests range from high-domed and rigid to low and flexible, and Phormosoma is more depressed than a stout Palaeechinus. Those outlines are grown skeletal forms, not sessile drops shaped by gravity and the pull of the tube feet.

For a cylindrical vessel at constant pressure and wall stress, thickness scales with radius, and large arteries roughly follow that pattern while pressure falls toward the capillaries. Arterioles are thick-walled relative to their lumen, so small arteries are not disproportionately thin; only capillaries match the thin-wall end of the claim.

Laplace’s relation for uniform wall stress makes thickness inversely proportional to mean curvature, and the left-ventricular apex is both sharply curved and relatively thin. Fiber architecture and the crescentic right ventricle depart from a single constant, so the inverse law is an approximation inside each chamber.

Mean systemic pressure is several times mean pulmonary pressure, on the order of six, while peak systolic pressure is closer to five times. Left-ventricular wall thickness is about three times the right-ventricular free wall, not six or seven times.

Arterial diameters and branching approximate an economy that balances pumping work against the cost of blood volume, so circulation is arranged toward minimum effort. Minimum wall area is not the same optimum and is not achieved independently of that tradeoff.

Small side branches tend to leave a parent artery at a large angle and large branches at a small one, and equal daughters diverge symmetrically. Measured angles scatter around those rules rather than locking to 70–90 degrees for every fine vessel.

A path that minimizes cumulative energy loss can obey a refraction-like condition relating the branch angle to the two loss rates. The accepted optimum from pumping power plus blood volume is a relation among the vessel radii, not the cosine rule as the general arterial law.

Lift, drag, and structural loads of swimming and flying forms can be calculated and measured. Crypsis, warning colours, and mimicry have also been demonstrated by experiment, so the contrast that colour adaptations cannot be shown is unwarranted.

Fresh cortical bone carries substantial load in both tension and compression, which lets a bone act as tie or strut. Longitudinal compressive strength is typically about one and a half times tensile strength, near 190–200 megapascals against about 130, so the stated near-equality and the older kilogram-per-square-millimetre figures are somewhat too close and too low.

Bending stiffness of a given amount of material is greatest when that material is far from the neutral axis, which a thin-walled tube provides in every direction. Albatross wing bones, feather quills, and reed stems are built that way.

Femoral cortex is thick along the diaphysis and thins toward the metaphyses, in the same broad region where bending moments of a loaded column are high. The thickness profile is not a simple graph of the bending-moment diagram, because gait loads and the cancellous ends reshape the shaft.

In the femoral neck and similar loaded bones, compressive and tensile trabecular arcades follow the principal stress trajectories and meet at roughly right angles, as in a crane-head diagram. The match is anatomical and mechanical, with local departures from a perfect stress drawing.

Orientations aligned with principal stress experience no shear and are mechanically favoured. Trabeculae reach those orientations by resorption and deposition sensed by osteocytes, not by being shoved into line as loose rods.

After a malunion changes the load paths, cancellous bone is progressively rebuilt along the new stress trajectories, including away from the fracture. Basic bone shape is also inherited, and full remodeling takes months to years rather than a complete replacement within a few weeks.

Sustained mechanical load stimulates bone-forming cells, and a fibula that inherits the tibia’s load hypertrophies toward the tibia’s thickness. Muscle, skin, and supporting plant tissues also thicken or reorient under load, through cellular signaling rather than an unmediated physical growth law.

A standing quadruped’s spine, loaded between the limb girdles with the head and trunk as opposing arms, behaves more like a double cantilever beam than like a masonry arch. Muscles and the limbs do carry some longitudinal force, so the bridge analogy is useful rather than strict.

Standing horses and elephants support about 55–60 percent of body weight on the forelimbs, and camels about two-thirds. Llamas are nearer the horse fraction than two-thirds, so the forelimb bias is real but the llama figure is high.

Supraspinous ligaments act as the tension chord, vertebral centra as the compression chord, and the neural spines separate them like a girder web. Spine height is greatest where bending moments are large, without being strictly proportional at every station.

Heavy heads and necks are accompanied by tall neural spines over the withers, as in bison and horses. Anteaters, Diplodocus, kangaroos, and Iguanodon, with the mass or the cantilever shifted rearward, have their tallest spines over the loins and sacrum.

Whales, seals, and sea-cows lack the peaked withers and haunch spines of terrestrial relatives, consistent with buoyancy removing those cantilevers. Their neural spines have not vanished entirely, and the pelvis of aquatic birds is specialized rather than simply weak and straight.

Cod and haddock stiffen the vertebral axis with a dorsal spine series and paired lateral processes, and three equally spaced struts would give uniform resistance. The angles are only roughly near 120 degrees, and the tail of a fish is organized by neural and haemal spines opposite one another.

The vertebral beam of a large dinosaur is shallow relative to a steel cantilever designed for the same static load. Extra depth would raise stiffness, and an animal column has to flex, so the shallower proportions match a strength-flexibility compromise.

Trabeculae and cortical robusticity are strongly aligned with habitual stress so as to limit shear. The shapes and arrangement of whole bones are also set by developmental patterning and ancestry, so the skeleton is only partly a diagram of stress.

Scapulae and vertebrae are readily reshaped by locomotor loads, and one such bone, similar or different, is weak evidence for or against relationship. Basilosaurus is in fact a stem whale, which illustrates the same caution: a whale-like scapula is consistent with kinship but does not by itself establish it.

New habits often shift suites of correlated skeletal parts together, and phenotypic integration makes graded, multi-part change common. Mosaic evolution also changes single elements while neighbours stay put, so modifications are not generally spread over the whole body.

Both organisms and inorganic bodies depart from ideal circles and catenaries because several forces act at once. Heredity, development, and selection make an additional difference in how living form is generated and preserved.

Among close relatives, a large share of shape difference is allometric change in relative lengths and widths. Discrete gains and losses of parts, meristic changes, and surface characters also separate species, so proportion is not the main cause in general.

Some closely related fishes, crustaceans, and skulls differ by a smooth, nearly global warp of a coordinate grid. Many comparisons need localized deformations, so a simple symmetrical Cartesian map is not the general rule.

A whole-body coordinate transformation shows that related fishes often differ in an integrated way. That description does not show a single physical growth law, nor that selection is limited to independent characters; selection acts on correlated suites as well.

Fossils in folded and cleaved rock are commonly flattened by tectonic shear, often close to simple shear. Distorted specimens have repeatedly been named as separate species and sometimes as separate genera.

Ox, sheep, and giraffe cannon bones are the same metapodial element graded mainly by slenderness: the sheep’s shaft is substantially narrower than the ox’s at comparable length, and the giraffe’s is narrower still. Articular and cross-sectional details differ as well, and the one-third and two-thirds figures are approximate.

A velocity field that is radial and tangential about a fixed basal point can draw outlines from lanceolate through ovate to cordate as the tangential component increases. Dicot blades grow by distributed plate and marginal meristems, and cordate bases involve localized lobe growth, so the ratio is a geometric illustration rather than the developmental rule.

Begonia leaf asymmetry is produced by faster growth on one side of the midrib, so the two halves are unequal versions of one lamina rather than unrelated outlines. A constant proportion between angles to equal radii is a plausible idealization, not a demonstrated identity for the two sides.
